'''Min Chen''' is an [[Australians|Australian]] plant physiologist. She is a full professor and [[Australian Research Council]] Future Fellow in the School of Biological Sciences at the University of Sydney. Her research is primarily concerned with elucidating the molecular and biochemical mechanism of the energy-storing reactions in [[photosynthetic]] organisms, especially the function of novel [[photopigments]] in oxygenic photosynthetic bacteria.

==Early life and education==

She was born in [[Dalian]], [[China]] and educated in [[Northeast Normal University]], China - BSc in 1984 and MSc in 1987 - and received her PhD in 2003 from [[University of Sydney]].<ref name="i576">{{cite web | title=Australian Society of Plant Scientists » 2013 Goldacre recipient Professor Min Chen | website=Australian Society of Plant Scientists  | date=29 March 2025 | url=https://www.asps.org.au/awards/peter-goldacre-award/2013-goldacre-recipient-professor-min-chen | access-date=16 April 2025}}</ref>

==Research==
Her research found that [[chlorophyll f]] has an absorption maximum at 706nm [[in vitro]], which suggests that oxygenic photosynthesis can be extended even further into the [[infrared]] region, which may open up associated bioenergy applications. Red-shifted chlorophylls could be used extend light capture in crop plants.<ref>{{cite web|last=Burdick|first=Alan|url=http://archive.onearth.org/print/7949|title=Power Plants|date=23 November 2010|work=OnEarth|publisher=National Resources Defense Council}}</ref>   Chen is the University of Sydney node leader of Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Translational Photosynthesis.<ref name=ARC>{{cite web|title=Chief Investigators & Partner Investigators|url=http://photosynthesis.org.au/chief-investigators-partner-investigators/|website=Translational Photosynthesis|access-date=13 December 2014}}</ref> The function of Chlorophyll f in photosynthetic reactions is uncertain and the ecological distribution of chlorophyll f remains unknown.<ref>{{Cite journal |doi = 10.1126/science.1191127|pmid = 20724585|title = A Red-Shifted Chlorophyll: Fig. 1|journal = Science|volume = 329|issue = 5997|pages = 1318–1319|year = 2010|last1 = Chen|first1 = Min|last2 = Schliep|first2 = Martin|last3 = Willows|first3 = Robert D.|last4 = Cai|first4 = Zheng-Li|last5 = Neilan|first5 = Brett A.|last6 = Scheer|first6 = Hugo|s2cid = 206527174}}</ref>

==Awards==
In October 2011, Chen was awarded the [[Prime Minister's Prizes for Science|Science Minister’s Prize for Life Scientist of the Year]],<ref>[http://www.innovation.gov.au/Science/InspiringAustralia/PrimeMinistersPrizesforScience/Recipients/2011PrizeRecipents/Pages/2011ScienceMinistersPrizeforLifeScientistoftheYear.aspx 2011 Science Minister's Prize for Life Scientist of the Year] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120229045107/http://www.innovation.gov.au/Science/InspiringAustralia/PrimeMinistersPrizesforScience/Recipients/2011PrizeRecipents/Pages/2011ScienceMinistersPrizeforLifeScientistoftheYear.aspx |date=2012-02-29 }}</ref> for her role in discovering a new form of chlorophyll, called [[chlorophyll f]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Australian scientists discover first new chlorophyll in 60 years|url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/746430779/ |publisher=Xinhua News Agency|date=20 August 2010|location=Woodside, United States}}</ref> In 2013 she was recipient of the Robin Hill Award of the International Society for Photosynthesis Research<ref>{{cite web|url=http://photosynthesisresearch.org/page-1853064|title=Awards presented at PS16, St Louis - August 2013|publisher=International Society of Photosynthesis Research|access-date=2014-10-31|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181107075211/http://www.photosynthesisresearch.org/page-1853064|archive-date=2018-11-07|url-status=dead}}</ref> and in the same year awarded the Peter Goldacre Award by the Australian Society of Plant Scientists.<ref name="i576"/>
